bodyText:
What is the SDLC?

The Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) is a structured process for planning, building, testing and maintaining software. It divides development into phases so that each stage is completed in an organized way, reducing cost, errors and project failure.

The Phases

  • Planning and feasibility: the problem is defined and a feasibility study checks whether the project is technically, economically and operationally viable.
  • Analysis: requirements are gathered from users and stakeholders and documented.
  • Design: the system architecture, database design and user interface are planned.
  • Implementation: programmers write the code according to the design.
  • Testing: the software is checked for defects and verified against the requirements.
  • Deployment: the finished software is installed and released to users.
  • Maintenance: the software is corrected, adapted and improved after delivery.

Maintenance is generally the longest phase of the life cycle, because software must keep working as user needs, hardware and laws change over time.

bodyText:
The Waterfall Model

The waterfall model, described by Winston Royce in 1970, is a linear sequential model: each phase must be finished before the next begins, like water flowing down steps. It is simple to manage and works well when requirements are clear and fixed, but it is rigid: returning to an earlier phase is difficult and expensive, and the user only sees working software near the end.

The Spiral Model

The spiral model, proposed by Barry Boehm in 1986, is risk-driven. Development proceeds in repeated loops, and each loop has four parts: determine objectives, identify and resolve risks, develop and test, and plan the next iteration. Prototypes are often built to reduce risk. It suits large, complex, high-risk projects but is more expensive and complex to manage than simpler models.

Agile Development

Agile development is iterative and incremental: software is built in small cycles and delivered frequently, with continuous feedback from users. The Agile Manifesto was written in 2001 by seventeen software developers. Its values favour individuals and interactions, working software, customer collaboration and responding to change over rigid processes and documentation. Scrum, developed by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, is the most widely used agile framework: work is organized into short sprints, typically two to four weeks long, with daily stand-up meetings and a review at the end of each sprint.

Other Models

The V-model pairs each development phase with a matching testing phase, forming a V shape. The prototype model builds an early working mock-up to clarify requirements. The RAD (Rapid Application Development) model, introduced by James Martin in 1991, uses workshops and reusable components to deliver software quickly.

bodyText:
Why Testing Matters

Testing checks whether software behaves as required and finds defects before users do. As Edsger Dijkstra observed, testing can show the presence of bugs, but never their absence. Testing is performed at several levels, each checking a different scope of the system.

Levels of Testing

  • Unit testing: tests the smallest testable parts, such as individual functions or classes, usually by the developers themselves.
  • Integration testing: tests modules combined together, checking that their interfaces work correctly.
  • System testing: tests the complete, integrated system against the requirements, including performance and security.
  • User Acceptance Testing (UAT): the final check by users or customers, confirming the system meets their needs before it is accepted.

Other Testing Terms

Alpha testing is done in-house by the development team in a controlled environment, while beta testing is done by real users in their real environment. Black-box testing checks behaviour without knowledge of the internal code, whereas white-box testing uses knowledge of the internal structure. Regression testing re-runs earlier tests after a change to make sure nothing broke, and smoke testing is a quick check that the basic functions work.

bodyText:
Software Documentation

Software documentation is the written material that accompanies software. User documentation, such as manuals and help guides, explains the software to end users. System documentation, including design documents, architecture diagrams and code comments, explains the software to developers who must maintain it. Good documentation reduces dependence on individual programmers, makes maintenance cheaper and helps new team members understand the system.

Software Maintenance

Maintenance is the modification of software after delivery to correct faults, improve performance or adapt it to a changed environment. It is the longest and most costly part of the life cycle. Lientz and Swanson classified maintenance into four types. Corrective maintenance fixes discovered defects. Adaptive maintenance adapts the software to changes in its environment, such as a new operating system or new laws. Perfective maintenance improves performance or adds features requested by users. Preventive maintenance changes the software to prevent future problems, for example by restructuring code.

bodyText:
Requirements Engineering

Requirements engineering is the process of discovering, documenting and validating what a system must do. It begins with elicitation, gathering needs from stakeholders, meaning anyone affected by the system. The requirements are then analyzed for conflicts, specified in a document, and validated to confirm they are correct and complete.

Functional and Non-Functional Requirements

Functional requirements describe what the system must do, for example 'the system shall allow users to log in'. Non-functional requirements describe quality attributes, such as performance, security, reliability and usability: for example, 'the system shall respond within two seconds'. A useful way to capture requirements is a use case, which describes an interaction between a user and the system.

The SRS Document

The Software Requirements Specification (SRS) is the formal document that records the requirements. The IEEE 830 standard gives its recommended structure. A good SRS must be complete, consistent, unambiguous, verifiable and traceable: every requirement should be testable and traceable back to its source. The SRS becomes the agreement between developers and customers and the basis for design and testing.
